title: Surface Area and Nets Grade 6: Draw, Fold, Add the Faces + Free Quiz
meta_title: Surface Area and Nets Grade 6 + Free Quiz
meta_desc: Learn surface area and nets in Grade 6: recognise nets of cubes, cuboids and prisms, then add every face to find total surface area. Free quiz inside.
excerpt: A net is just a solid unfolded flat. Once a Grade 6 child sees that, surface area stops being a formula to memorise and becomes something you can literally count — add up every face and you are done. Here is how to teach the skill, with a quiz.
author: Sachin Sharma
content:
Hand a Grade 6 student an empty toothpaste carton and ask them to cut along the edges and flatten it. What they get is a net — the box opened out into six flat rectangles. That single moment does more for understanding surface area and nets in Grade 6 than any formula on the board, because now the child can see every face at once and simply add up their areas. No memorising ‘2(lb + bh + hl)’ before they know what it means. You count the faces first; the shortcut comes later.

This is a skill-practice guide, not a theory dump. The goal is that your child can look at a flat pattern and say ‘that folds into a cube’, and can find the total surface area of a cuboid by adding six rectangles. Give it ten minutes with some squared paper and a pair of scissors.

What a net actually is

A net is a two-dimensional shape that folds up into a three-dimensional solid. Every face of the solid appears exactly once in the net, laid flat and joined along edges. A cube unfolds into six identical squares. A cuboid (a box shape) unfolds into six rectangles — three matching pairs. A triangular prism unfolds into two triangles and three rectangles.

The counter-intuitive bit, and the part children love, is that one solid can have many different nets. A cube has eleven distinct nets — eleven ways to arrange six squares that still fold back into a cube. In my experience the fastest way to make this stick is to let a child cut out a wrong arrangement and try to fold it. When two squares overlap or a face is missing, they remember it far better than if you had just told them.

The quick fold test

Before adding any areas, a child should be able to tell whether a flat pattern is a valid net. Two checks do most of the work:

  • Count the faces. A cube net needs exactly six squares — no more, no fewer.
  • Fold it in your head (or for real). No two faces should land on top of each other, and there should be no gap left uncovered.

Finding surface area straight from the net

Here is the whole method for total surface area at Grade 6 level: unfold the solid into its net, find the area of every face, and add them together. That is it. Because the net shows all the faces flat, there is nothing hidden and nothing to double-count.

Take a cuboid that is 5 cm long, 3 cm wide and 2 cm tall. Its net has six rectangles in three matching pairs. Work out one of each pair, then double:

Face pairDimensionsArea of one faceBoth faces
Top and bottom5 cm × 3 cm15 cm²30 cm²
Front and back5 cm × 2 cm10 cm²20 cm²
Two ends3 cm × 2 cm6 cm²12 cm²

Add the last column: 30 + 20 + 12 = 62 cm². That is the total surface area, and the child got there by adding faces — not by trusting a formula they cannot picture. Later they will notice the pattern is exactly 2(lb + bh + hl), and by then the formula is a summary of something they already understand.

Cubes are the easy case

A cube has six identical square faces, so surface area is just the area of one face times six. For a cube with edge 4 cm, one face is 4 × 4 = 16 cm², and the whole surface is 16 × 6 = 96 cm². I always start children here, because one number does all the work and it builds confidence before the cuboid’s three different pairs arrive.

Nets of prisms

A triangular prism is the next step up and it trips people because the faces are not all rectangles. Its net has two triangular ends and three rectangles for the sides. To find the surface area you add the two triangle areas to the three rectangle areas. The method has not changed at all — unfold, find each face, add — there are just two different shapes of face to handle.

One honest caveat: watch the units. If lengths are in centimetres, areas must be written in cm², not cm. Marks are lost on this more than on the arithmetic itself. Drill the small square-two into every answer from the start.

Common slip-ups worth naming

  • Forgetting a face — usually the hidden bottom or back. Counting faces on the net stops this.
  • Counting a face twice. Each face appears once in the net; if you drew it twice, refold to check.
  • Multiplying the wrong two sides for a rectangular face — each face uses only two of the three dimensions.
  • Mixing up surface area (add the faces, answer in cm²) with volume (multiply length × width × height, answer in cm³).

A ten-minute practice routine

Squared paper, scissors, and one solid object a day. Monday: draw and fold a cube net. Tuesday: a cuboid net and add its six faces. Wednesday: sketch a triangular prism net. Thursday: a mix, where the child has to decide which faces exist before adding. Friday: two word problems — how much card to make a box, how much paint for a block. Making the child choose the faces themselves, rather than being handed the layout, is where the skill really sets.

Try the quiz, then the worksheet

The eight-question quiz below checks exactly these skills — spotting valid nets, counting faces, and adding areas to find total surface area for cubes and cuboids. Let your child work through it and read the explanations for anything they miss. When they are ready for longer written practice, the printable worksheet at the end has graded net-and-surface-area questions with a full answer key.

quiz.title: Grade 6 Surface Area and Nets Quiz
quiz.intro: Eight questions on nets, counting faces and finding total surface area of cubes and cuboids. Choose an answer for each, then press Check my score.
quiz.about: Grade 6 nets and total surface area

questions.q: How many square faces does a net of a cube have?
questions.explanation: A cube has six identical square faces, so its net is made of exactly six squares.

questions.q: A cuboid net is made up of which shapes?
options: Six rectangles in three matching pairs
questions.explanation: A cuboid has six rectangular faces that come in three matching pairs: top/bottom, front/back and the two ends.

questions.q: A cube has an edge of 3 cm. What is its total surface area?
questions.explanation: One face is 3 × 3 = 9 cm². There are six faces, so 9 × 6 = 54 cm².

questions.q: Which solid has a net made of two triangles and three rectangles?
questions.explanation: A triangular prism has two triangular ends and three rectangular sides, so its net shows two triangles and three rectangles.

questions.q: A cuboid is 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm. What is the area of its top face?
questions.explanation: The top face measures length × width = 4 × 3 = 12 cm².

questions.q: What is the total surface area of a cuboid 4 cm by 3 cm by 2 cm?
A flat pattern has seven squares joined together. Can it be the net of a cube?
options: No, a cube net needs exactly six squares
Yes, if they are all the same size
questions.explanation: A cube has six faces, so a valid cube net must have exactly six squares. Seven is one too many.

questions.q: In what units should the surface area of a solid measured in centimetres be written?
questions.explanation: Surface area is an area, so it is measured in square units — cm² when the lengths are in centimetres.

faq.q: What is a net in Grade 6 maths?
faq.a: A net is a flat, two-dimensional pattern that folds up into a three-dimensional solid. Every face of the solid appears once in the net, so a cube net is six squares and a cuboid net is six rectangles.

faq.q: How do you find surface area from a net?
faq.a: Find the area of every face shown in the net, then add them all together. Because the net lays every face out flat, nothing is hidden and nothing gets counted twice.

faq.q: How many different nets does a cube have?
faq.a: A cube has eleven distinct nets — eleven ways to arrange six squares so they still fold back into a cube. Letting a child cut and fold a wrong arrangement is the best way to show why some patterns fail.

faq.q: What is the difference between surface area and volume?
faq.a: Surface area is the total area of all the faces, found by adding them and measured in square units like cm². Volume is the space inside, found by multiplying length × width × height and measured in cubic units like cm³.
